meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it: an information-operations watch (kind "info-ops": official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns), a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cyber and influence below the threshold of war, and the targeted side's responses) or an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation, its gains, the enemy's response and what it shows). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.
types.hybrid attack: Physical sabotage, arson, cable or pipeline damage, cyber attacks, GPS jamming, drone or airspace incursions and other deniable attacks below the threshold of war.
types.defensive response: The targeted side's practical countermeasures: arrests, expulsions, airspace closures, deployments, new laws and alliance consultations.
types.territorial change: Ground or settlements gained or lost, with who reports it and whether it is independently confirmed (geolocated footage, ISW).
types.official claim: A command's or ministry's claim of gains, enemy losses or prisoners that has not been independently confirmed.
types.counterattack: The opposing side's counterattacks, reinforcements or renewed assaults in the operation's sector.
types.tactic or capability: A tactic, weapon or enabler used in the operation (drones, electronic warfare, converted vehicles, shaping strikes).

items.whyNow: A US-announced energy truce collapsed within four days as Russia massed 39 ballistic missiles on Kyiv's grid on 14 Oct while Ukraine was reportedly out of Patriot interceptors and facing Starshield speed limits; it is the clearest live test of what happens to layered air defence and dispersed energy repair when key enablers are withdrawn.
changes: 15 Oct: Ukraine's Navy said a Neptune strike destroyed six Su-34M bombers at Borisoglebsk (General Staff confirms six damaged, not independently established); Zelensky said the block on refinery strikes is "out" after Russia kept hitting energy during Kyiv's pause, Russia reported a drone-caused fire at a Ryazan refinery, and CNN reported Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors (single source) (AeroTime, Newsweek, Meduza/CNN).

14 Oct: Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv, damaging 26 power facilities and leaving 600,000 without power, as SpaceX speed limits on Starshield/Starlink were reported; the UK pledged a £45m air-defence package including faster Lightweight Multirole Missiles against jet drones, and the 3rd Army Corps claimed Vivaldi's fourth stage: 101 sq km including Kolodiazi, 277 sq km in all (Kyiv Independent, ISW).

13 Oct: Likely Russian drones struck two civilian vessels in Bulgaria's EEZ, which Bulgaria's prime minister called absolutely unacceptable; a drone hit a university in Rivne injuring 30, ballistic missiles reached Kyiv without early warning, and Trump declined to blame Moscow for breaking the truce (ISW, Kyiv Independent).

12 Oct: Zelensky said Russia hit six energy facilities and offered a full energy ceasefire on reciprocity, while Peskov rejected a 60-day ceasefire and offered only a one-day pause; Russia's MoD claimed Ukrainian forces encircled in Dobropillia, which ISW found unsupported beyond limited infiltration (ISW).

11 Oct: Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire that neither side had confirmed and Russia struck the Kharkiv thermal power plant hours later; Ukraine hit a Yandex data centre in Vladimir Oblast, its third in four days, and Sochi airport (Al Jazeera, ISW).

10 Oct: Russian glide bombs on Zaporizhzhia residential buildings killed 16 (at least 23 civilians over 10–11 Oct per ISW) and Trump told Zelensky to "stop" refinery strikes a day after the US licensed Russian diesel imports; Ukraine damaged at least seven tanks at a Rostov-on-Don oil terminal (Al Jazeera, ISW).

next.text: Whether the Kremlin formally accepts any energy-strike moratorium (it has offered only a one-day pause, 12 Oct) or Washington acts on its reported threat to restrict intelligence sharing and early warning after Ukraine lifted its refinery-strike pause on 15 Oct.

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A daylight Russian jet-drone raid hit Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences and killed five people across Ukraine, Zelensky said Russia had begun additional mobilisation as Putin enlarged the armed forces by 15,500, and the 3rd Army Corps closed Vivaldi's third stage with 51 square kilometres, three settlements and over 250 prisoners taken using converted BTR-60s as kamikaze vehicles.

Russia struck hydroelectric, thermal, substation and energy-storage sites around Kyiv, killing seven, and a drone hit the grounds of the Kyiv nuclear research institute, as ISW judged Russia's Winter 2026–27 strike campaign had begun.

Russian drones struck Kyiv's Southern Bridge while a metro train was crossing, the first attack on a Kyiv bridge of the full-scale war, as Ukraine reported the first combat use of its FP-7 ballistic missile.
On Putin's birthday Russia fired 48 cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and 130 drones across Ukraine, killing at least 30 people, more than 20 of them in an apartment block in Pryluky.
A Russian glide bomb killed 33 people on two minibuses in Kramatorsk, the deadliest single strike of the year, as a drone strike knocked out a Yandex data centre in Russia's Ryazan region.
Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire that neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed, and Russian forces struck the Kharkiv thermal power plant hours later.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at energy sites around Kyiv and Kharkiv, leaving 600,000 without power, as the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth Vivaldi stage of 101 square kilometres north of Lyman.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds and favours Ukraine around Lyman: the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth stage of 101 sq km on 14 Oct, which ISW ties to a months-long intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian rear areas, while ISW found no evidence on 11–13 Oct for Russian claims around Dobropillia, where Russia depends on small infiltration groups. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating is borne out, but the contest now turns on enablers rather than jamming: Starshield speed limits reported on 13–14 Oct threaten jet-drone interception, Patriot stocks were reported exhausted on 15 Oct (single source), and improvised layers appeared, such as drone escorts protecting tanks on 11 Oct.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens on both sides. Russia's 39-ballistic-missile strike on 14 Oct hit 26 power facilities and cut power to 600,000, and Ukraine answered by ending its refinery pause on 15 Oct after hitting Yandex and Sberbank data centres and the Borisoglebsk bomber base. Repair and replacement throughput, not protection, remains the deciding variable.

watches.label: Shadow-war watch
watches.title: Russia–Europe shadow-war watch
watches.trigger: Russian helicopter and drone incursions into Poland, Romania and Moldova, 23–24 Sep 2026
watches.question: Is Russia escalating a shadow war against Europe below the threshold of open war (sabotage and arson, cyber attacks, undersea cable and pipeline damage, GPS jamming, drone and airspace incursions, shadow-fleet activity, espionage, assassination plots and influence or disinformation operations), through which channels and against whom, and how are European governments and NATO responding?

feed.query: (Russia OR Russian OR Kremlin OR GRU) (sabotage OR "hybrid war" OR "hybrid attack" OR "hybrid threat" OR "shadow war" OR "shadow fleet" OR "drone incursion" OR "airspace violation" OR "undersea cable" OR arson OR "GPS jamming" OR cyberattack OR espionage OR disinformation) (Europe OR European OR NATO OR Poland OR Germany OR Baltic OR Romania OR Finland OR Britain OR France OR Denmark OR Moldova)

findings.actor: EU Council working group; Poland, Sweden, Estonia (per Politico Europe via The Moscow Times)
findings.text: On 15 Oct 2026 The Moscow Times reported that EU states were weighing Limited Territorial Validity visas for Russians, prompted by an alleged August drone plot in Germany involving a Russian who entered on an Italian tourist visa; European Parliament President Metsola backed targeted restrictions. Nothing has been adopted, a Commission proposal is reportedly not due until early 2027, and the Irish Council presidency reportedly warned the measure might not stop the threats.

findings.actor: Unidentified drone operators (ISW: likely Russian); Bulgarian government
findings.tactic: Drone strikes on merchant ships in EEZ
findings.text: Early on 13 Oct 2026 drones hit the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3 about 18 nautical miles off Bulgaria and sank the cargo ship HS Dignity off Krapets, leaving 11 crew missing, a week after a 6 Oct strike in the same zone that sank a ship. Nothing was intercepted; Sofia summoned Russia's ambassador and asked NATO and the EU for help, but did not formally attribute the attack, and ISW assessed Russia is extending risk-taking from airspace incursions to maritime strikes.

On 12 Oct 2026 the French Navy boarded the sanctioned tanker DF Peak more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion on suspicion of a false Benin flag, and is escorting it for inspection; it is at least the fifth Russia-linked tanker France has stopped since 2024. The boarding worked as an interdiction, but no confiscation or criminal liability has yet been established, and Moscow called it piracy.

findings.actor: Polish ABW and police with German BKA
findings.text: On 12 Oct 2026 two Turkish men were detained in Nürtingen, Germany, at Poland's request over the 23 Sep arson at an Exatel Starlink ground station near Warsaw; Poland said it had recordings, fingerprints and DNA and had "no doubt" Russian services were behind it. The cell was identified within three weeks and faces sabotage charges, but the attack itself was not prevented and Poland says others were likely involved.

findings.actor: Moldovan air surveillance against an unidentified strike drone
findings.text: On the night of 10 Oct 2026 a drone carrying an explosive payload crashed into a tree near Geamăna, Anenii Noi district, about 20 km inside Moldova; police neutralised the warhead and no one was hurt. Moldova's Defence Ministry said its air surveillance had recorded no unauthorised flight, so the incursion went undetected; Chisinau did not attribute it, while ISW judged it likely Russian and part of a normalising pattern.

findings.actor: NoName057(16) (pro-Russian hacker group); Italian Foreign Ministry
findings.text: On 8 Oct 2026 the pro-Russian group NoName057(16) was believed to be behind a distributed denial-of-service attack on the Italian Foreign Ministry website, and checks were run on embassy and consulate sites abroad. The ministry said the attack was "effectively mitigated" without causing any disruption. Italy said it would work with Romania and other EU states to propose designating those behind such attacks.

On 8 Oct 2026 the EU prolonged its sanctions regime for Russia's hybrid and destabilising activities until 9 Oct 2027, keeping asset freezes and travel bans on 80 individuals and 20 entities (up from 47 and 15 a year earlier). The Council cited "continued and intensified" Russian hybrid activity, so the listings have grown but the evidence does not yet show them deterring operations.

On 8 Oct 2026 Britain added 12 tankers to its shadow-fleet list, taking UK-sanctioned vessels to 645, alongside sanctions on oil producers Zarubezhneft and INK Capital and on crypto and payment networks. Designation keeps rising, but the reporting gives no evidence on whether listed vessels have actually stopped trading.

On 8 Oct 2026 Sandu and Speaker Igor Grosu announced legislation to allow Moldova to manufacture drones and air-defence equipment at home, because purchases abroad face long waiting lists; Sandu reportedly counted nine Russian drone violations in seven days and more than 20 in September (single source). The step follows Moldova's inability to intercept the objects crossing its airspace and has not yet produced any capability.

findings.tactic: Broad destabilisation replaced by targeted sabotage
findings.text: On 7 Oct 2026 PET lead analyst Josefine Christensen said Russia had moved from planning to carrying out sabotage against Danish firms that supply Ukraine, focusing on weapons and drone production, after concluding that its earlier broad destabilisation had failed to curb Western support. Operations since early summer rely on people recruited via Telegram, escalating from photography tasks to sabotage, with failed recruits quickly replaced. No specific incident or damage was named, and the Russian embassy denied the claims.

findings.tactic: Missile and drone overflight of Moldova
findings.text: On the morning of 3 Oct 2026 three Banderol-type missiles and two drones crossed Moldovan airspace during a strike on Ukraine and fell in several districts, starting a fire but causing no casualties. Nothing was intercepted, and Chisinau's response was limited to summoning Russia's ambassador for the second time in a week, so the incursion achieved its effect unopposed.

assessment.text: Between 3 and 15 Oct 2026 Russia's most effective tools stayed the cheapest: unattributed drones. Strikes sank merchant ships in Bulgaria's Black Sea EEZ on 6 and 13 Oct with nothing intercepted, and a warhead-carrying drone crashed near Anenii Noi on 10 Oct without Moldova's air surveillance recording any intrusion. Sabotage has been superseded rather than abandoned: Danish PET said on 7 Oct that broad destabilisation gave way to targeted attacks on Ukraine's suppliers by disposable proxies. Defenders win mainly after the event. Poland and Germany caught the two alleged Starlink-station arsonists within three weeks (12 Oct), France boarded the false-flag tanker DF Peak (12 Oct), and Italy absorbed a NoName057(16) DDoS on 8 Oct. Bulgaria responded only by summoning Russia's ambassador and appealing to NATO. Sanctions listings and the visa curbs debated on 15 Oct remain unproven as deterrents, and attribution gaps still blunt collective responses at sea and in the air.

watches.title: Operation Vivaldi watch (Lyman counteroffensive)
watches.trigger: 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi reveals Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive north of Lyman, 15 Sep 2026
watches.question: Can Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corps counteroffensive north of Lyman, keep regaining ground and disrupt Russia's planned pincer on the Donbas fortress belt (Lyman–Sviatohirsk in the north, Dobropillia in the south, converging on Barvinkove), how is Russia responding with counterattacks, reserves and narrative, and what does it show about restoring manoeuvre under drone-saturated conditions?

feed.query: ("Operation Vivaldi" OR "3rd Army Corps" OR "Third Army Corps" OR Biletskyi OR Lyman OR Sviatohirsk OR Svyatohirsk) (Ukraine OR Ukrainian OR Russia OR Russian OR offensive OR counteroffensive)

findings.tactic: Dedicated deception feeding false battlefield picture
findings.text: UNITED24 reported on 15 Oct 2026 that the corps ran a dedicated unit that fed Russian forces, including higher command, a deliberately false picture of the battlefield, alongside suicide ground robots used behind Russian lines. The corps credits this with surprise and with exhausting Russian reserves in its sector; the account is the corps' own and not independently confirmed.

On 14 Oct 2026 the corps said the fourth and final "season" of Vivaldi had retaken 101 km² including Zelena Dolyna, Lypove and Kolodiazi, for 277 km² and 16 settlements overall, and claimed about 3,000 Russian losses in the phase (8,000 in total, 250+ prisoners). The area and loss figures are claims; ISW's 13 Oct report placing Russian attacks "toward Kolodyazi" without gains is consistent with Ukrainian control, and Biletskyi said the operation continues in another form.

findings.actor: Russian command (1st Guards Tank Army, per Biletskyi)
findings.tactic: Shifting tank-army units from Kupiansk to Lyman
findings.text: Biletskyi said on 14 Oct 2026 that Vivaldi halted the Russian West grouping's offensive and forced some 1st Tank Army units to move from the Kupiansk direction to Lyman, easing pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi and securing the Kharkiv–Sloviansk highway. The redeployment did not stop the fourth-phase gains; the transfer itself is a Ukrainian claim not confirmed by ISW.

findings.tactic: Concentrated assaults on Lyman and Kolodyazi
findings.text: ISW reported on 13 Oct 2026 that Russian forces concentrated attacks on Lyman and north toward Kolodyazi on 12-13 Oct but did not advance while Ukrainian forces kept counterattacking. A Russian Western Grouping source also claimed attacks southeast of Borova, for which ISW saw no evidence of gains.

findings.tactic: Eastern frontal push on the Fortress Belt
findings.text: ISW's 12 Oct 2026 assessment showed average daily Russian attacks in the Sloviansk direction falling from about 14 in August to 5 in September and 3 in October, and in the Kramatorsk direction from 3 to 0.3. ISW linked the drop partly to Vivaldi's cascading effects and Ukrainian counterattacks, but said Russia may also be pausing before a fall offensive, so the eastern prong is stalled rather than abandoned.

findings.actor: Russian forces on the Zherebets River line
findings.text: ISW reported on 11 Oct 2026 that Russian attacks around Lyman on 10-11 Oct gained nothing as Ukrainian forces counterattacked north and south of the town, while a Russian milblogger claimed Russian troops still held central Zarichne. On 10 Oct a milblogger called the Zherebets settlements vital for logistics and said losing Zarichne and Yampil would make a new Lyman offensive "impossible"; neither side's control of Zarichne is geolocated.

ISW's 10 Oct 2026 report cited geolocated footage of 9 Oct implying a Ukrainian advance northwest of Borova Andriivka, and a Kremlin-affiliated milblogger acknowledged that Ukraine had liberated Rai-Oleksandrivka east of Kramatorsk, linking it to Vivaldi's success near Lyman. The same milblogger said Russian forces were trying to retake the village.

findings.tactic: Massed fire to block Russian reserves
findings.text: ISW's 9 Oct 2026 assessment relayed the corps' account that massed artillery kept Ridkodub, Zelena Dolyna and Kolodyazi under continuous fire, preventing Russia from bringing up reserves to retake lost positions, and that HIMARS destroyed over 20 guns and two Buk systems (claims). Zelena Dolyna and Kolodiazi were declared taken on 14 Oct, and geolocated footage of 8 Oct showed a Ukrainian advance west of Zarichne toward the Zherebets; ISW also observed Russia's 71st Unmanned Systems Regiment entering the sector.

findings.actor: Ukrainian 66th Mechanized Brigade and 3rd Army Corps UGV units
findings.tactic: Ground robots for resupply and demining
findings.text: A Kyiv Independent field report published on 8 Oct 2026 said the 66th Brigade's 20 UGV operators now run 100-150 logistics missions a month, each robot carrying about half a tonne and surviving mine hits, while other UGVs clear mines ahead of infantry. Soldiers said resupply now arrives within hours and drivers are no longer exposed. The figures come from the units themselves.

findings.tactic: Lancet and glide-bomb interdiction of logistics
findings.text: The same 8 Oct 2026 Kyiv Independent report said Ukrainian logistics movements in the Lyman sector stop whenever a Lancet threat is reported and that Russia uses guided bombs against supply targets, while drone crews expect retaliation as priority targets. This slows but has not halted Ukrainian resupply.

findings.actor: Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping of Forces
findings.text: ISW reported on 7 Oct 2026 that Ukrainian forces were counterattacking toward the eastern bank of the Zherebets River and that Russian forces were struggling to contain Vivaldi's gains. A Kremlin-affiliated milblogger citing Rybar conceded that Ukrainian manpower and drone superiority was preventing Russian forces from consolidating around Lyman, which ISW said matched its observations of continued successful Ukrainian counterattacks.

findings.actor: Russian command (as read from Pushilin's remarks by ISW)
findings.tactic: Northern pincer on the Fortress Belt
findings.text: On 5 Oct 2026 Russian-installed DNR head Denis Pushilin said Slovyansk and Kramatorsk would very likely be the last territory Russia takes in Donetsk Oblast, which ISW read as an implicit admission that Vivaldi had curtailed the northern thrust. ISW found no Russian gains in the Lyman direction on 4-5 Oct, suggesting the wide encirclement via Lyman and Sviatohirsk has given way to a frontal approach from the east.

assessment.text: Vivaldi's method held through its fourth phase. The corps declared Zelena Dolyna, Lypove and Kolodiazi retaken on 14 Oct, claiming 101 km² and 277 km² overall. Those totals are unconfirmed, but ISW's 13 Oct report of Russian attacks toward Kolodyazi failing fits Ukrainian control. What worked was shaping before assault: massed artillery and HIMARS fire kept Russian reserves away from the target villages (9 Oct), a dedicated deception unit misled Russian command (15 Oct, single source), and ground robots carried logistics (8 Oct). Russian countermeasures largely failed. Assaults around Lyman made no confirmed gains on 10-13 Oct, and reported transfers of 1st Tank Army units from Kupiansk did not stop the advance (Ukrainian claim). The northern pincer via Lyman has been superseded. Russia is now contesting the Zherebets River line, with Zarichne disputed on 10-11 Oct, and its eastern attacks toward Sloviansk fell to about three a day by 12 Oct. Lancet interdiction remains the main contested counter as the corps shifts to a new, undisclosed form of operations.

changes: 15 Oct: Thai army spokesman Maj Gen Winthai Suvaree rejected Cambodia's UNHCR figures, saying the 650,000 were people who moved into shelters temporarily and that Thailand counts about 4,600 people (900-plus households) in three Sa Kaeo areas it says are Thai territory needing security controls, and pointed to the 2000 MOU and the Joint Boundary Commission; the same day Cambodia's foreign ministry said both sides must make no public statement on conciliation outcomes until the Commission's press release, and AKP reported the UN had published Ambassador Keo Chhea's letter rebutting Thailand's UN General Assembly claims (Nation Thailand; AKP; Khmer Times).

14 Oct: The second meeting of the UNCLOS Conciliation Commission opened at the Peace Palace in The Hague under Katrina Cooper, with Prak Sokhonn and Sihasak Phuangketkeow as agents; Cambodia restated that it seeks a single maritime boundary treaty, or joint development pending one, or failing both a Commission report with recommendations (AKP; Cambodianess).

14 Oct: At the UNHCR Executive Committee in Geneva, Cambodian envoy Ke Sovann replied to Thai Permanent Representative Benjamin Sukanjanajtee, denied laying new anti-personnel mines, said recent blasts that hurt Thai soldiers were in old documented minefields, and demanded Thailand stop 'unlawful activities' in areas it occupies (AKP; Cambodian claims).

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

The first UNCLOS conciliation session in Singapore (14–16 September) closed with Cambodia tabling three settlement options and Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; a second meeting was set for The Hague on 14–18 October.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Anutin told the UN General Assembly that Thailand regretted Cambodia's turn to UNCLOS conciliation after the two leaders had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally, and urged joint work on border security, demining and scam networks.

Prak Sokhonn told the UN General Assembly that the conflict had seriously eroded trust, that over 20,000 Cambodians still cannot return home, that Thailand should implement the December agreements and resume Joint Boundary Commission demarcation, and that the Charter sets no separate standard for powerful states.

Hun Manet said the United States had asked Thailand to stop escalatory actions and encroachment on Cambodian territory, and Thailand's foreign ministry denied it the same day, conditioning any boundary commission meeting on a border secure from landmines and transnational crime.

The second UNCLOS conciliation meeting opened at the Peace Palace in The Hague as Cambodia and Thailand clashed at the UNHCR Executive Committee in Geneva over the more than 20,000 Cambodians Phnom Penh says cannot return home.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status is borne out on the line but not in the argument: no exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty was reported from 2 to 15 Oct, yet on 14 Oct Cambodia denied at the UNHCR Executive Committee that it had laid new mines, and Crisis Group warned on 9 Oct that with demining cooperation suspended a minor incident could set off a third round (search summary only). The mine question remains the likeliest spark. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired: observers visited An Ses on 7 Oct and met Cambodian commanders in Battambang on 14 Oct, but the Thai army said on 15 Oct that three Sa Kaeo areas are Thai territory needing security controls, so local consolidation is now argued as sovereignty that monitoring can record but not reverse.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted: the contest has moved to multilateral legal forums rather than ASEAN, through Geneva on 13–15 Oct, a Cambodian letter the UN published, and The Hague from 14 Oct, where the agreed rule against public comment (15 Oct) is the first external restraint on messaging. Adaptability stays Low.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger status holds and the trigger looks further off: no strike has been found since the 4 Oct Caribbean strike that killed four, and coercion now runs through the courtroom, with the 8 Oct torture indictment and the 15 Oct not-guilty pleas moving the decisive sovereignty question, Maduro's head-of-state immunity, to a hearing dated 17 Nov or 17 Dec by conflicting reports. Legitimacy is now contested over who sets the election calendar rather than over the US role. Chinese maritime militia vessel 9622 deployed 22 sampans around Philippine-held Kota Island, one within about 250 metres of the shore, and its master encircled the Philippine response boats and claimed the area as Chinese before all the vessels left.

China's Liaoning carrier group sailed between Okinawa and Miyako into the western Pacific and launched and recovered aircraft about 155 miles south of Ishigaki inside Japan's exclusive economic zone, five days before the US-Japan Keen Sword exercise, as Japan scrambled fighters and sent a destroyer and patrol aircraft to track it.

timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025; each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day and India later rejects Pakistan's account as 'the usual prevarication'.

The Indian Army says a joint operation at Korag–Yousmarg in Budgam killed Pakistan-based LeT commander Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa, wanted for the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, and recovered his body at Palmaidan.

Pakistan's army spokesman presents a retired special-forces havildar named Muhammad Asif alive in Rawalpindi, calls India's Korag claim a staged 'false flag' and warns of 'very harsh retribution' for any attack built on such claims.

India's Border Security Force shoots dead two Pakistani men on the Punjab border, which India calls an infiltration attempt and Pakistan an unprovoked killing of villagers, and each side summons the other's envoy the next day.
Pakistan's Army Rocket Force Command tests an extended-range version of the Fatah-4 terrain-hugging ground-launched cruise missile, without disclosing its new range.
A landmine blast near the Line of Control in Poonch kills four men whom Pakistani officials call villagers repairing a water pipeline and Indian Army sources call Lashkar-e-Taiba infiltrators.
Pakistan's Army Rocket Force Command test-fires the Fatah-2 Extended Range, billed as a hypersonic ballistic missile able to defeat missile defences, its second missile test in a week.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status is borne out at low intensity: the 2 Oct BSF shooting and the 12 Oct Poonch landmine, which killed four men whom Pakistani officials call villagers and Indian Army sources call infiltrators, produced rival narratives rather than fire, and no Line of Control firing was reported. Lethal incidents are recurring but are being absorbed by summons and statements, not answered kinetically. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established status holds and is hardening: Rajnath Singh's 15 Oct warning of a 'stronger response' to any Pakistan-origin attack restates a strike threshold, while the duelling Poonch accounts show attribution contested from the first hour.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested status is borne out more sharply: the Army Rocket Force Command fired an extended-range Fatah-4 cruise missile on 6 Oct and a Fatah-2 ER, billed as hypersonic and able to defeat missile defences, on 13 Oct, both with ranges undisclosed, building conventional stand-off options below the nuclear line. India's 14 Oct UN push on Pakistan-administered Kashmir carries the contest into forums. Adaptability remains High in missile reach, not doctrine.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's regional command near Kyaikto, killing at least six including Air Force defector Nay Win Aung, as the Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt on the Maei pass at Mindon, Malaysia sets 29 Sep to begin deporting Myanmar migrants, Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand, a Delhi court lets the foreign drone trainers leave India and an MNDAA delegation opens Chinese-pressed talks in Naypyidaw.

A junta fighter jet drops two bombs on the main wholesale market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, at about noon, killing at least 33 people and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a senior rescue official's count, the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing, with no comment from the military.

Junta air strikes hit two displacement camps in Ponnagyun Township, Rakhine State, on 4 and 5 October, killing eight and wounding 13 by the Arakan Army's and a local youth group's count, a week after the Kyauktaw market strike.

Junta warships, artillery and aircraft begin a week of failed landing attempts on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base near Sittwe, and by 14 October the Arakan Army still holds the island and has taken outposts on the city's edge, by local accounts.

Min Aung Hlaing met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya on a two-day official visit and pledged to take back verified Myanmar nationals as soon as possible, with a second phase of 3,524 returns awaiting a date.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status is borne out: jets struck Ponnagyun camps on 4–5 Oct, a Shwebo monastery on 11 Oct, Mindon on 8–12 Oct and Bilin near the Mon–Karen border on 13 Oct, yet airpower still fails to deliver ground. Junta landings on Ngapyi Island from 7 Oct were repelled and the Arakan Army took outposts at Amyint Kyun on 14 Oct (AA-sourced, unverified); the regime's only clear gain was Maiza in Sagaing on 9 Oct. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out in a new setting: the AA reportedly used drones with artillery against warships and landing craft on the Kaladan on 8–9 Oct, turning cheap systems into a riverine anti-landing defence, while both sides used drones around Sittwe and in the 11 Oct Bhamo push (single source), so diffusion is two-sided.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced: the regime harassed Rakhine fishermen at sea on 12 Oct to tighten the coastal blockade, fought for the Sagaing–Kachin road and rail corridor, and converted displacement into diplomatic credit when Malaysia hailed returns on 14 Oct. Adaptability stays High.

items.whyNow: Houthi missiles killed 12 at Riyadh's main airport on 10 Oct, reached Aramco in Dhahran more than 1,100 km away on 13 Oct and hit Aden's presidential palace on 15 Oct, exposing a stretched Saudi air-defence layer. With Hormuz at its most dangerous, Saudi energy and the Red Sea bypass route that Singapore-bound flows lean on sit inside the fight.
changes: 15 Oct: Houthi missiles and drones hit Aden's al-Maashiq presidential palace complex for the first time in this conflict, killing five and wounding 16 per the health minister (AFP sources: at least four), with the Houthis calling it a Saudi operations headquarters; the coalition said Riyadh airport had been attacked 20 times in October, killing 17 and wounding 333, claimed a cruise missile intercepted over Medina (Houthis deny) and the EU postponed its Riyadh summit with Gulf states (Al-Monitor/Reuters, France 24, CBS live).

14 Oct: Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, condemned the attacks and pledged Iraqi territory would not be used to target the kingdom; the coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh, the WFP said fighting is cutting food aid to about 800,000 people, and a Houthi spokesman said the group would welcome mediated talks while repeating maximalist demands (Al-Monitor, Al Jazeera, CBS live, Critical Threats).

13 Oct: A missile or debris set fire to an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, more than 1,100 km from Houthi territory, as Saudi defences intercepted at least eight missiles aimed at Riyadh, Dhahran, Haradh and al-Kharj (four injured in Riyadh); Saudi jets struck Houthi fuel depots in Sanaa, Dhamar and Hudaydah after warning civilians (Critical Threats, Al Jazeera).

12 Oct: The Houthis fully encircled Taiz City and took al-Misrakh district, and Saudi Arabia extended Riyadh airport's closure after another attack; WSJ sources said Saudi air defences are stretched and prioritise palaces and energy infrastructure (Critical Threats).

10 Oct: A missile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid airport, killing 12 and wounding 309 per Saudi authorities, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in over a decade; the airport closed and several airlines suspended Saudi services, and Trump said of US strikes on the Houthis 'We may. We're going to look at it' (Al Jazeera, Critical Threats).

9 Oct: Government-aligned forces seized Jabal Kahbub and reportedly Perim Island and al-Aradi near Bab al-Mandab (unconfirmed), as the Saudi command claimed 136 Houthi targets destroyed and round-the-clock air support; Iranian drones hit an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp near Erbil on 8 Oct, the first such strike since the US exit, and Iraq said it expects to begin trucking crude to Syria's Baniyas from mid-October (Critical Threats, The National).

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.

After the Houthis fire a mixed missile and drone barrage at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh and Saudi Arabia intercepts six ballistic missiles, President Macron announces French soldiers, radars and air-defence systems for the Yanbu terminal and the Makkah pact foreign ministers agree in New York to convene their chiefs of staff.
The US-led coalition ended its 12-year mission in Iraq as the last US troops left, while Iraqi militias refused to disarm and a new breakaway militia with Iranian support was reported.
Yemeni government forces launched a Saudi-backed offensive to retake Mokha and the Bab al-Mandab shore, with the coalition citing 100 jets in support, while the Houthis denied losing ground.

A Houthi missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid airport, killing 12 people and wounding 309 by Saudi count, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade, and the airport was shut.

Houthi missiles hit the presidential palace complex in Aden for the first time in this conflict, killing five people by the health minister's count, as the coalition reported 20 attacks on Riyadh airport in October.

text: Long-range attack versus layered protection is borne out as Rising · Contested and still favours the attacker: a missile struck Riyadh airport's terminal on 10 Oct, killing 12, an Aramco building in Dhahran more than 1,100 km from Houthi territory burned on 13 Oct, and missiles hit Aden's presidential palace on 15 Oct. WSJ sources reported on 12 Oct that Saudi defences are stretched and now prioritise palaces and energy over airports, so rationing coverage is the defender's adaptation, and the coalition's own count of 20 attacks on Riyadh airport this month shows its cost. Maritime disruption versus route resilience is Established · Contested but contested on land more than at sea: government forces reportedly took Perim and ground near Bab al-Mandab on 9 Oct, unconfirmed and disputed by the Houthis, while no Houthi attack on merchant shipping appeared in the week's reporting.

Regional basing versus militia targeting stays Established · Contested in a political rather than kinetic form: Iraq's prime minister pledged in Riyadh on 14 Oct that Iraqi soil would not be used against the kingdom, yet Iranian drones struck a Kurdish camp near Erbil on 8 Oct, the first since the US exit. Adaptability is High on the first topic and Medium on the others.
